speaker: Doctor
text: I am Dr. Agent. I see you have blisters on your forearm and ulcers on your mucosal surfaces; to determine the cause, have you had any recent sun exposure, and do you have any history of autoimmune diseases like lupus or pemphigus?

speaker: Patient
text: 50-year-old female. The patient reports the appearance of blisters on her forearm 3 days ago, accompanied by pain in her left cheek when eating and pain during sexual intercourse for the past week. She has been hiking in the woods recently but denies contact with poison ivy. She has a history of hypertension and osteoarthritis, recently started taking captopril, and discontinued meloxicam 2 weeks ago. Family history includes pernicious anemia and Graves' disease.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the details; since you were recently hiking in the woods, have you noticed any new blistering or skin changes specifically on your hands or arms, and do you experience extreme fatigue or joint pain?

REQUEST TEST: CBC with differential, ANA, Anti-Ro/SSA, Anti-La/SSB, and Complement levels (C3, C4).
REQUEST IMAGES: Dermatology photos of forearm lesions.

speaker: Doctor
text: The test results for CBC, ANA, and complement levels are normal, which makes systemic autoimmune diseases like lupus or pemphigus less likely. Given your recent initiation of captopril, do you notice any itching or burning sensations specifically at the sites of the blisters? Also, do you have any mouth sores or genital pain currently?

speaker: Patient
text: includes pernicious anemia and Graves' disease.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Drug-induced bullous pemphigoid or mucocutaneous reaction to captopril.

The negative autoimmune panel and lack of sun-induced lesions make SLE and pemphigus vulgaris unlikely, pointing toward an adverse reaction to the new medication you started. Did the blisters or mucosal pain appear within a few weeks of starting the captopril, and have you noticed any rash in areas where the medication touches the skin?
